To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the number of founder HIV viruses can be reliably estimated from truncated data, that this number can be used to estimate the vaccine effect, and that the vaccine effect can be estimated even if the distribution of the founder virus number is completely unspecified.
we have developed a method for estimating the efficacy of a vaccine that incorporates the number of founder virions that cause the first infection.

(i) we develop a new approach for incorporating information on the number of founder virions in vaccine clinical trials; (ii) the approach is applicable to any distribution on 0,…, and can be used with truncated data, even if the placebo group and vaccine group distributions of the number of founder viral particles are completely unspecified; (iii) the approach can also incorporate covariate information; and (iv) we apply our method to an HIV vaccine clinical trial conducted in injecting‐drug users.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the estimation of a vaccine's effectiveness at reducing the mean number of founder viruses per exposure.
incorporating founder virus information into vaccine clinical trials.
incorporating the information on the founder virus in vaccine clinical trials and developing new methods of estimating vaccine efficacy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the vaccine was associated with a 50% reduction in the number of infective exposures, but that the reduction in infecting virions was only 20% (95% confidence interval: −3%, 40%).
the vaccine reduced the mean number of founder viruses by 0.6 per exposure, but this statement would be misleading if the mean number of founders was 0 for both placebo and vaccine.
the vaccine reduced the risk of HIV infection by about 30%.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the number of founder virions can be a very useful addition to vaccine clinical trials.
the number of infectious virions is an important quantity that can help us to better understand vaccine efficacy.

the methods developed here provide a more powerful approach to analyzing vaccine trials than the standard Cox proportional hazards model, and that the methods are robust to misspecification of the distribution of founder virus counts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the inclusion of information on the number of founder virions can greatly improve the precision of vaccine efficacy estimates.
, in addition to the time to infection, the number of infectors can be used to improve vaccine trial designs and analysis.
incorporating information on the number of virions in the analysis of vaccine trials may lead to more efficient estimation of vaccine efficacy.
